papers.title: Data Visualization in the Neurosciences: Overcoming the Curse of Dimensionality
papers.summary: A critique of visualization practice in neuroscience, based partly on a survey of 288 articles, with a checklist for figures that reveal rather than conceal data. It is especially relevant to labeling, showing raw distributions, avoiding gratuitous 3D, and communicating uncertainty.
papers.catalog_blurb: Survey and practical checklist for clearer, more honest neuroscience figures.
key_findings: In the surveyed neuroscience figures, labeling and uncertainty depiction were especially weak for 3D displays.
The authors recommend informative displays that expose data structure and uncertainty instead of relying on standard decorative forms.
limitations: The journal sample is from 2010 and the article is a short NeuroView rather than a comprehensive systematic review.

findings.claim: The survey covered 288 articles and found only 20% of 3D graphics portrayed uncertainty.
The article frames its recommendations as design choices that reveal data rather than hide it.

related.reason: Later empirical survey of ERP visualization practice.
Parallel audit of figures in clinical-trial reports.

papers.title: A Survey and Task-Based Quality Assessment of Static 2D Colormaps
papers.summary: Surveys static two-dimensional colormaps, defines seven quality measures, maps them to seven analysis tasks, and evaluates 22 reimplemented maps. Its main contribution is a reproducible, task-based way to choose a 2D colormap rather than assuming one palette is universally best.
papers.catalog_blurb: Task-based measures and selection guidance for static 2D colormaps.
key_findings: Elementary tasks impose conflicting colormap requirements, while results for synoptic tasks are more consistent.
Ten evaluated colormaps passed all described tasks without exclusion on black or white backgrounds.
limitations: The assessment is measure-based and static; some published maps had to be approximately reimplemented.

findings.claim: The work maps seven quality measures to seven multivariate analysis tasks.
Ten colormaps were robust across all described tasks and backgrounds.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.description: Summary of assessed designs and guidance.

related.reason: One of the influential 2D color-map constructions assessed.
Early empirical work on two-variable color maps.

papers.title: Uncertainty Visualization: Why Might It Fail?
papers.summary: Explains the gap between enthusiasm for uncertainty visualization and its limited use in practice through an industrial underground-asset mapping case. The paper broadens the explanation beyond encoding technique to data availability, trust, standards, cognition, and organizational constraints.
papers.catalog_blurb: Why uncertainty visualizations fail to transfer from research into practice.
key_findings: Uncertainty displays are limited when uncertainty metadata are incomplete, inconsistent, or themselves distrusted.
Perceptual issues interact with social and organizational constraints, so technical encodings alone cannot ensure adoption.
limitations: A short work-in-progress paper grounded mainly in one industrial case.

findings.claim: The abstract identifies data scope, confidence, and perceptual or cognitive confusion as limiting factors.
The utility case reports incompatible confidence schemes and patchy metadata across organizations.

related.reason: Empirical study of why authors omit uncertainty.
Broad review of technical and pipeline challenges.

papers.title: A Review of Uncertainty in Data Visualization
papers.summary: A broad review organized around a visualization-pipeline reference model. It distinguishes visualizing uncertainty already attached to data from uncertainty introduced by filtering, mapping, interpolation, and rendering, then surveys methods for scalar, vector, and other data.
papers.catalog_blurb: Pipeline-based review of uncertainty sources and visualization methods.
key_findings: The pipeline model separates uncertainty in input data from uncertainty introduced by visualization processing.
The review argues that crisp displays can imply unjustified confidence and that uncertainty must be considered throughout the pipeline.
limitations: A 2012 snapshot of a fast-moving literature; it is a review rather than a comparative user study.

findings.claim: The reference model distinguishes visualization of uncertainty from uncertainty of visualization.
The conclusion reviews both data uncertainty and uncertainty created by the visualization process.

related.reason: Domain-specific medical-imaging survey.
Foundational geospatial uncertainty framework.

papers.title: Value-Suppressing Uncertainty Palettes
papers.summary: Introduces value-suppressing uncertainty palettes (VSUPs), which allocate fewer distinguishable value bins as uncertainty grows. A crowdsourced evaluation compares these palettes with conventional bivariate and juxtaposed maps for identification and decision tasks.
papers.catalog_blurb: Uncertainty-aware bivariate palettes that suppress value resolution when uncertainty is high.
key_findings: VSUPs caused participants to weight uncertainty more strongly and avoid highly uncertain choices.
Superimposed maps outperformed juxtaposed maps in the identification task, and discrete bins outperformed continuous color for precise identification.
limitations: Results depend on the experimental tasks, risk framing, and chosen palette construction.

findings.claim: VSUPs reduced value resolution at high uncertainty and encouraged more cautious decisions.
Superimposed displays achieved 58% versus 51% accuracy for juxtaposed displays in the reported task.

related.reason: Alternative uncertainty display evaluated through judgment tasks.
Task-oriented design of bivariate map palettes.

papers.title: Makie.jl: Flexible High-Performance Data Visualization for Julia
papers.summary: Describes Makie.jl, a Julia plotting ecosystem combining GPU-backed interactive graphics, publication-quality vector output, reactive Observables, layouts, and extensibility through multiple dispatch. It is implementation context rather than evidence about a specific visualization encoding.
papers.catalog_blurb: Architecture and capabilities of the Makie.jl visualization ecosystem.
key_findings: Makie offers one interface for interactive, animated, raster, and vector visualization.
Reactive Observables and extensible conversion and plotting pipelines support live updates and custom data types.
limitations: A software paper describing capabilities at publication time, not a usability or performance comparison.

findings.claim: Makie combines GPU-powered interactive visualization with publication-quality vector graphics.
The project positions itself as filling Julia gaps in control, performance, and interactivity.

sections.label: Motivation
sections.description: Gap in the Julia plotting ecosystem.

related.reason: Domain-specific EEG visualization software.
Grammar-based uncertainty visualization software.

papers.title: Confidence Intervals for fMRI Activation Maps
papers.summary: Documents a common misreading of thresholded fMRI activation maps and proposes color encodings based on confidence-interval bounds. The designs aim to show plausible effect-size ranges and support comparisons between conventionally active and inactive voxels.
papers.catalog_blurb: Confidence-interval maps to reduce binary misreadings of fMRI activation.
key_findings: Conventional thresholded maps invite the false inference that colored voxels reliably differ from uncolored voxels.
Confidence-interval-based maps improved respondents' ability to judge whether locations differed reliably.
limitations: The proposed encodings are initial designs demonstrated on limited datasets and survey tasks.

findings.claim: The paper identifies omitted trends and probable effect-size ranges as key failures of standard activation maps.
Survey results show fewer mistaken comparisons with the confidence-interval displays.

sections.label: Survey comparison
sections.description: Interpretation results for two proposed methods.

related.reason: Broader survey of uncertainty-aware medical imaging.
General image-aggregation approach that can yield interval-like encodings.

papers.title: diegr: Dynamic and Interactive EEG Graphics
papers.summary: The CRAN reference manual for the diegr R package. It documents dynamic and interactive high-density EEG graphics, data manipulation, averaging, confidence intervals, scalp and topographic plots, and animations; it is API documentation, not an empirical paper.
papers.catalog_blurb: Reference manual for interactive and animated EEG graphics in R.
key_findings: The package supports exploratory and communicative analysis of spatiotemporal high-density EEG signals.
Its documented workflows include pointwise confidence intervals, jackknife averages, topographic plots, and 3D scalp representations.
limitations: Package documentation dated August 2026; verify behavior against the installed package version.

findings.claim: The package description states its focus on interactive plots and animations for temporal-spatial EEG signals.
The manual demonstrates confidence-interval waveforms and jackknife topographic averages.

related.reason: Survey of practitioner needs and EEG visualization tools.
EEG analysis toolbox with scalp-time inference.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware Visualization in Medical Imaging: A Survey
papers.summary: Surveys uncertainty-aware visualization across medical-image acquisition, transformation, visualization, and clinical applications. It evaluates approaches against requirements, considers how methods can form end-to-end pipelines, and identifies modality and workflow gaps.
papers.catalog_blurb: Pipeline-oriented survey of uncertainty visualization in medical imaging.
key_findings: Uncertainty affects every stage of medical imaging and can influence diagnosis, planning, and treatment.
Many approaches use separate uncertainty images, which can be hard to correlate with anatomy in clinical work.
limitations: Coverage and ratings reflect the literature available in 2021 and a small group of clinical collaborators.

findings.claim: The survey organizes uncertainty-aware methods by imaging stages and applications.
The discussion identifies separate color-coded uncertainty images as difficult to correlate in routine use.

related.reason: Concrete uncertainty design for fMRI maps.
Empirical evaluation in biomolecular visualization.

papers.title: Voice AI
papers.summary: A GWDG newsletter article describing the KISSKI Voice-AI transcription and live-captioning service. It reports use of Whisper large-v3 on local HPC infrastructure, privacy-oriented handling, and integration with BigBlueButton for lectures and meetings.
papers.catalog_blurb: Service overview for privacy-oriented transcription and live captioning at GWDG.
key_findings: Voice-AI uses Whisper large-v3 for transcription, translation, and caption generation.
The service is positioned as a privacy-conscious alternative and can feed captions into BigBlueButton shared notes.
limitations: The PDF is a full newsletter issue; only pages 3 and 5–7 concern Voice-AI, and claims are service-provider descriptions rather than an evaluation.

findings.claim: The editorial introduces Voice-AI as real-time transcription and video captioning with a privacy-oriented motivation.
The article describes Whisper large-v3, privacy handling, and BigBlueButton integration.

sections.label: Voice-AI article
sections.description: Model, features, privacy, and captioning integration.

related.reason: Another software or service reference in the collection.
Another non-evaluative tool reference.

papers.title: Hypothetical Outcome Plots Outperform Error Bars and Violin Plots for Inferences about Reliability of Variable Ordering
papers.summary: Introduces hypothetical outcome plots (HOPs), animations of sampled outcomes intended to let viewers reason through counting and visual integration. In a 288-person experiment, HOPs substantially improved judgments about the ordering of two or three uncertain quantities compared with error bars and violin plots.
papers.catalog_blurb: Animated samples improve multivariable probability judgments over common static displays.
key_findings: HOPs yielded much lower error for two-variable ordering-probability judgments.
For many single-variable questions, accuracy was similar across HOPs, error bars, and violin plots; HOPs were not uniformly superior.
limitations: Animated displays can require more viewing time and the study used specific distributional tasks with online participants.

findings.claim: The abstract reports higher accuracy with HOPs for two- and three-quantity judgments.
All tested two-variable plots showed much lower mean absolute error with HOPs.

related.reason: Task-based evaluation of another uncertainty encoding.
Practical treatment of HOPs and uncertainty graphics.

papers.title: Why Authors Don't Visualize Uncertainty
papers.summary: Uses a survey of 90 visualization authors and interviews with 13 influential designers to characterize why uncertainty is often omitted. The study surfaces tensions between acknowledged value and practical reluctance, including audience concerns, workflow costs, lack of conventions, and uncertainty about consequences.
papers.catalog_blurb: Practitioner evidence on the social and practical causes of uncertainty omission.
key_findings: Authors often value uncertainty communication while believing it may confuse audiences or weaken a message.
The paper calls for usable text and visual guidance plus a clearer account of the implicit inferences viewers make when uncertainty is omitted.
limitations: Convenience survey and purposively selected interview samples do not estimate population prevalence.

findings.claim: The study combines 90 survey responses with 13 interviews to characterize omission rationales.
The discussion recommends aligning displays with the inference model authors actually use.

related.reason: Earlier account of adoption barriers in an industrial setting.
Documents persistent omission in a policy-relevant map literature.

papers.title: Communicating Uncertainty to Policy Makers in Maps: A Systematic Scoping Review of Meaningful to Misleading Current Practice
papers.summary: A PRISMA-compliant scoping review of 66 studies using maps for climate-sensitive infectious disease in the Asia-Pacific. It evaluates whether uncertainty is connected to the visual evidence used for policy and finds that explicit visual communication remains rare.
papers.catalog_blurb: Systematic review showing widespread omission of uncertainty from policy-facing disease maps.
key_findings: Only 3 of 66 included studies visualized uncertainty in their maps.
Forty-three studies omitted uncertainty or mentioned it only in disconnected text, and 11 confined it to captions.
limitations: Restricted to peer-reviewed Asia-Pacific climate-sensitive infectious-disease studies and qualitative synthesis.

findings.claim: The review screened 2,826 records and included 66 studies.
Only three included studies visualized uncertainty; most omitted it or separated it from the maps.

sections.label: Abstract
sections.description: Scope, review design, and headline findings.

related.reason: Systematic audit of uncertainty reporting in ecosystem science.
Review of user studies evaluating geospatial uncertainty displays.

papers.title: Understanding Uncertainty in Forest Resources Maps
papers.summary: Reviews uncertainty in forest-resource maps and tests kriging, quantile random forests, and simulation on laser-scanning data with simulated responses. It separates pixel-level uncertainty from uncertainty in landscape-level characteristics and highlights the lack of usable joint prediction-and-uncertainty displays.
papers.catalog_blurb: Methods and visualization gaps for uncertainty in forest-resource maps.
key_findings: Kriging captured pixel-level uncertainty in the test case, whereas quantile random forest slightly underestimated it.
Simulation can estimate uncertainty for complex landscape-level characteristics that pixelwise intervals do not answer.
limitations: The method comparison uses a controlled simulated response and may not generalize to all forest-map models.

findings.claim: The highlighted results contrast accurate kriging with slight QRF underestimation and motivate simulation.
The conclusion calls for broader use of uncertainty estimation and better joint visualization tools.

related.reason: Policy and interpretation risks in maps.
GIS implementation for attribute uncertainty.

papers.title: ERP CORE: An Open Resource for Human Event-Related Potential Research
papers.summary: Introduces ERP CORE, a standardized collection of paradigms, experiment scripts, processing pipelines, and data from 40 participants for seven common ERP components. It supplies reproducible reference data and analysis choices for developing and testing EEG methods.
papers.catalog_blurb: Standardized paradigms, pipelines, and open data for seven ERP components.
key_findings: ERP CORE covers N170, MMN, N2pc, N400, P3, LRP, and ERN with optimized paradigms and predefined analysis parameters.
The resource is intended for direct study use, data-quality benchmarking, and testing new analytic techniques.
limitations: The sample is 40 neurotypical young adults; direct reuse still requires checking fit to a new population and question.

findings.claim: The resource includes standardized materials and data for seven widely used ERP components.
The authors describe validated pipelines as reducing errors and researcher degrees of freedom.

related.reason: ERP visualization practice and recommendations.
Complementary EEG analysis toolbox.

papers.title: ggdist: Visualizations of Distributions and Uncertainty in the Grammar of Graphics
papers.summary: Presents ggdist as an extension of ggplot2 that maps functions of probability distributions directly to visual aesthetics. The paper organizes a broad family of slabs, intervals, lineribbons, and dot displays and uses a distributional lens to connect Bayesian and frequentist uncertainty graphics.
papers.catalog_blurb: A distributional grammar for expressive uncertainty graphics in ggplot2.
key_findings: ggdist makes uncertainty designs beyond basic error bars, bands, and densities expressible within a grammar of graphics.
Distribution objects and confidence distributions provide a common interface across Bayesian and frequentist workflows.
limitations: Primarily a design and software paper; it does not claim every supported geometry is perceptually validated.

findings.claim: The abstract defines direct mappings from distribution functions to visual channels.
The three main geometry families are slabintervals, lineribbons, and dots.

related.reason: Another general construction for uncertainty graphics.
Empirical basis for sample-based distribution displays.

papers.title: How to Assess Visual Communication of Uncertainty? A Systematic Review of Geospatial Uncertainty Visualisation User Studies
papers.summary: Systematically reviews empirical user studies of geospatial uncertainty visualization. It characterizes their designs and findings, emphasizes that success depends on the user's task, and recommends task-centered typologies for more comparable evaluation.
papers.catalog_blurb: Systematic review and evaluation guidance for geospatial uncertainty user studies.
key_findings: Only a small part of uncertainty-visualization research had empirically evaluated proposed techniques.
Task-centered framing is necessary because analytical, decision, and exploratory goals impose different requirements.
limitations: The evidence base is limited to studies available through 2014 and is heterogeneous in methods and outcomes.

findings.claim: The review recommends task-centered typologies for systematic evaluation.
Analytical and exploratory tasks require different levels of tailoring and versatility.

related.reason: General visualization-evaluation scenarios.
One empirical comparison of thematic uncertainty methods.

papers.title: Geovisualizing Attribute Uncertainty of Interval and Ratio Variables: A Framework and an Implementation for Vector Data
papers.summary: Proposes a framework for showing attribute uncertainty in vector GIS data by extending bivariate mapping. An ArcGIS extension implements overlaid symbols on choropleths, color properties on proportional symbols, and composite proportional symbols.
papers.catalog_blurb: Bivariate GIS framework and ArcGIS tools for vector attribute uncertainty.
key_findings: The design chooses uncertainty encodings according to whether the mapped attribute uses choropleth or proportional-symbol representation.
The implementation provides three concrete tools inside a standard GIS environment.
limitations: The paper emphasizes framework and implementation rather than a large controlled user evaluation.

findings.claim: The abstract defines the framework and its three ArcGIS visualization tools.
The motivation is the lack of uncertainty tools in standard GIS environments.

related.reason: Uncertainty and visualization needs in resource maps.
Conceptual basis for geospatial uncertainty representation.

papers.title: Thematic Uncertainty Visualization Usability: Comparison of Basic Methods
papers.summary: Compares basic methods for displaying uncertainty in thematic soil maps through user tasks involving value, uncertainty, and their combination. The results stress that relative performance changes with task and that learning or ordering effects can influence apparent intuitiveness.
papers.catalog_blurb: User comparison of basic thematic-map uncertainty encodings.
key_findings: No single tested uncertainty method dominated all task types.
Whitening performed well in parts of the study, but the authors note that earlier exposure may have contributed.
limitations: The archived PDF text begins with publisher front matter and has imperfect multi-column extraction; consult the rendered PDF for exact tables and stimuli.

findings.claim: The results note that whitening's advantage may partly reflect prior exposure in the intuitiveness stage.
Combined value-and-uncertainty comparison was the most controversial task segment.

sections.label: Reference context
sections.description: Links to the broader uncertainty-visualization literature.

related.reason: Systematic review placing such user studies in context.
Another four-method uncertainty-visualization comparison.

papers.title: Empirical Studies in Information Visualization: Seven Scenarios
papers.summary: Derives seven visualization-evaluation scenarios from a review of more than 800 publications: work practices, visual analysis and reasoning, communication, collaboration, user performance, user experience, and algorithm performance. It tells researchers to choose goals and questions before methods.
papers.catalog_blurb: Seven goal-centered scenarios for choosing visualization evaluation methods.
key_findings: Evaluation scenarios distinguish what a study is trying to learn, not merely which method it uses.
Of 850 coded papers in the reported venues, 361 included evaluations that informed the seven-scenario framework.
limitations: The venue sample reflects information-visualization publication practice up to 2011 rather than all applied fields.

findings.claim: The abstract defines the seven scenarios and their use in study planning.
The conclusion reports 361 evaluated papers out of 850 surveyed and summarizes the framework.

related.reason: Methodology for problem-driven design studies.
Domain-specific review of uncertainty-visualization evaluations.

papers.title: Visualizing Uncertain Information
papers.summary: A foundational conceptual paper on uncertainty in GIS and cartographic visualization. It distinguishes data quality from uncertainty, considers Bertin's graphic variables, connects kinds of spatial uncertainty to map symbolization, and outlines interface strategies and evaluation needs.
papers.catalog_blurb: Foundational framework for representing and interacting with uncertainty in GIS.
key_findings: Exploratory GIS use requires uncertainty information because maps and computers otherwise invite unwarranted trust.
The paper frames representation choice through data-quality concepts, graphic variables, uncertainty types, and interaction.
limitations: Conceptual and pre-modern-GIS; many proposed directions require later empirical validation.

findings.claim: The paper distinguishes data quality from uncertainty and relates uncertainty to graphic variables and interfaces.
It warns that combining layers and flexible GIS processing can create substantial hidden uncertainty.

sections.label: Motivation
sections.description: Why GIS exploration needs uncertainty support.

related.reason: Later pipeline-based review across visualization domains.
Implementation of bivariate GIS uncertainty methods.

papers.title: The Art of Brainwaves: A Survey on Event-Related Potential Visualization Practices
papers.summary: Survey of 213 M/EEG practitioners about visualization tools, plot terminology, pain points, and preferences. It identifies inconsistent names, difficulty adding uncertainty, problematic colormap defaults, and produces recommendations for practitioners and tool developers.
papers.catalog_blurb: Large practitioner survey of ERP visualization tools, conventions, and problems.
key_findings: The community lacks consistent names for some common ERP plot types.
Thirty-two percent of respondents reported difficulty adding uncertainty to ERP plots, and rainbow maps remained unusually common in EEG.
limitations: Convenience sample and generally small reported effects; the authors explicitly advise cautious interpretation.

findings.claim: The survey included 213 practitioners and examined tools, challenges, uncertainty, and colormaps.
Thirty-two percent reported difficulty adding uncertainty to ERP plots.

related.reason: Earlier neuroscience-figure audit and guidance.
An EEG graphics package addressing some surveyed needs.

papers.title: Evaluating the Impact of Binning 2D Scalar Fields
papers.summary: Compares continuous and binned grayscale encodings for geospatial elevation fields across diverse tasks. The study shows a task-dependent speed–accuracy tradeoff: continuous encodings were often faster, while binned encodings matched or exceeded their accuracy.
papers.catalog_blurb: Task-dependent speed and accuracy tradeoffs for binned versus continuous scalar fields.
key_findings: Continuous encodings often reduced completion time but never produced higher accuracy than binned encodings in the tested tasks.
Binning is preferable when accuracy dominates; continuous encoding may help when speed dominates.
limitations: Uses grayscale elevation stimuli and specific tasks, so palette, domain, and working-memory demands may change results.

findings.claim: The abstract reports faster continuous encodings without an accuracy advantage.
The implications recommend binning for accuracy and continuous encoding for speed.

related.reason: Also finds task benefits from quantized color encodings.
Task-based evaluation of 2D color maps.

papers.title: LIMO EEG: A Toolbox for Hierarchical LInear MOdeling of ElectroEncephaloGraphic Data
papers.summary: Introduces the EEGLAB-compatible LIMO EEG toolbox for hierarchical linear modeling over electrodes and time while retaining single-trial variability. It supports robust bootstrap inference and multiple-comparison correction in a massive-univariate framework.
papers.catalog_blurb: Hierarchical, robust, scalp-by-time modeling toolbox for EEG data.
key_findings: LIMO EEG analyzes all space-time measurements without requiring hand-picked electrodes or time windows.
Its massive-univariate design is flexible and interpretable but does not directly model full spatial and temporal covariance.
limitations: Toolbox and software dependencies reflect 2011; the discussion notes covariance and computation limitations.

findings.claim: The toolbox accounts for single-trial variability using hierarchical linear models over space and time.
The discussion describes both flexibility and the limits of the massive-univariate approach.

related.reason: Standardized ERP paradigms and processing pipelines.
Spatial interpolation and scalp-current mapping method.

papers.title: Spherical Splines for Scalp Potential and Current Density Mapping
papers.summary: Derives spherical-spline methods for interpolating scalp potentials and approximating scalp current density. Relative to the authors' earlier thin-plate approach, it offers a simpler current-density derivation, faster computation, and better behavior in sparsely sampled scalp regions.
papers.catalog_blurb: Foundational spherical-spline interpolation for EEG scalp maps and current density.
key_findings: Simulation tests led the authors to select spline order m = 4 for their interpolation method.
The same framework supports smoothing noisy measurements and confidence intervals for approximated maps.
limitations: Short methods note based on idealized spherical projection and computing assumptions of its era.

findings.claim: The summary states advantages in derivation simplicity, speed, and sparse-electrode accuracy.
The paper describes smoothing for noisy measurements and confidence intervals for maps.

sections.label: Method motivation
sections.description: Relation to thin-plate splines and spherical projection.

related.reason: Statistical EEG analysis across electrodes and time.
Modern practice around ERP topographic visualization.

papers.title: A General Approach to Visualizing Uncertainty in Statistical Graphics
papers.summary: Treats a plot as a function of uncertain quantities, samples the induced distribution over rendered images, and aggregates those images into one uncertainty display. The framework generalizes overlay methods and can make confidence intervals and bands emerge without special-purpose plotting routines.
papers.catalog_blurb: General uncertainty graphics via resampling and pixel-level image aggregation.
key_findings: The method requires a base uncertainty distribution and ordinary plotting code, then operates on the resulting images.
It provides coverage guarantees for several common visual-inference tasks and an open-source IID reference implementation.
limitations: Raster-only proof of concept; anti-aliasing, intensity perception, color mixing, and dependence beyond IID data require care.

findings.claim: The abstract describes the distribution-over-images construction and emergent intervals or bands.
The conclusion states coverage guarantees and the link to standard inference.

sections.label: Conclusion
sections.description: Guarantees and relationship to overlay methods.

related.reason: General grammar for distributional uncertainty displays.
Sample-based display with empirical evaluation.

papers.title: Figures in Clinical Trial Reports: Current Practice & Scope for Improvement
papers.summary: Audits figures in 77 randomized-trial reports from five medical journals and develops practical guidance. Four types—flow diagrams, Kaplan–Meier plots, forest plots, and repeated measures—made up 92% of figures, but style and clarity varied widely.
papers.catalog_blurb: Audit and concrete guidance for figures in randomized clinical-trial reports.
key_findings: Trial reports averaged 2.3 figures and relied overwhelmingly on four recurring figure types.
The authors identify substantial room to improve labeling, display of statistical uncertainty, and consistency.
limitations: The sample covers three months in 2006–2007 and five general medical journals.

findings.claim: The abstract reports the 77-report sample, mean figure count, and four dominant types.
The discussion emphasizes diversity of practice and the importance of uncertainty intervals.

sections.label: Discussion
sections.description: Role of figures and practice variation.

sections.label: Guidance
sections.description: Recommendations including error bars and sample sizes.

related.reason: Comparable figure-practice audit in neuroscience.
Audit of uncertainty reporting in another scientific domain.

papers.title: A User Study to Compare Four Uncertainty Visualization Methods for 1D and 2D Datasets
papers.summary: Compares error bars, uncertainty-scaled glyphs, color-mapped glyphs, and uncertainty color-mapped onto a data surface using search and counting tasks on 1D and 2D data. The central result is interaction: effectiveness depends strongly on both task and dimensionality.
papers.catalog_blurb: Four-method user study showing that uncertainty-encoding performance is task-dependent.
key_findings: Performance differences among the four methods depended on the assigned task and dataset dimensionality.
Error bars were comparatively consistent, whereas surface coloring performed poorly for several tested tasks.
limitations: The archived annotated PDF has a broken font encoding, making extracted text largely unreadable; verify all details in the rendered PDF.

findings.claim: The garbled extracted abstract still identifies four methods, 27 users, and search and counting tasks.
The extracted closing discussion reports strong task dependence and comparatively consistent error-bar performance.

sections.label: Abstract (font-garbled)
sections.description: Study design and result outline; use the PDF image for authoritative reading.

related.reason: Another task-dependent comparison of uncertainty encodings.
Review of geospatial uncertainty user studies.

papers.title: Design Study Methodology: Reflections from the Trenches and the Stacks
papers.summary: Defines visualization design studies and derives practical methodology from 21 projects plus literature in HCI and social science. Its nine stages—learn, winnow, cast, discover, design, implement, deploy, reflect, and write—cover collaboration from problem selection through transferable lessons.
papers.catalog_blurb: Nine-stage methodology and pitfalls for problem-driven visualization design studies.
key_findings: A design study joins a real domain problem and users to abstraction, visualization design, validation, and reflection.
Task clarity and where information resides help determine whether a problem is suitable and what contribution is possible.
limitations: Methodological guidance synthesized from author experience, not a controlled comparison of research processes.

findings.claim: The abstract defines design studies and lists the nine-stage framework.
The methodology requires real users, real data, abstraction, and explicit design alternatives.

sections.label: Core criteria
sections.description: Analysis, real-world problem, and design requirements.

related.reason: Goals-first framework for choosing evaluation approaches.
Evaluation lessons in the uncertainty-visualization domain.

papers.title: Uncertainty Visualization for Biomolecular Structures: An Empirical Evaluation
papers.summary: Combines expert assessment with three crowdsourced studies (1,756 participants total) to evaluate nine metaphors for positional uncertainty across protein representations. It tests spontaneous association, directionality, and quantitative judgment instead of assuming familiar encodings are effective.
papers.catalog_blurb: Expert and large-scale perceptual evaluation of uncertainty metaphors for proteins.
key_findings: No tested metaphor was strongly and consistently associated with uncertainty without instruction.
Noise had clear directionality and relatively low absolute error, while the familiar sausage metaphor showed unintuitive directionality.
limitations: Studies used static 2D images; results may differ for interactive or stereoscopic 3D and for variants within each metaphor.

findings.claim: Three perceptual studies included 1,756 participants.
Fewer than 70% used any metaphor as intended; the sausage direction was below chance-like 50% accuracy.

related.reason: Survey of uncertainty methods in biomedical imaging.
Earlier comparative evaluation of uncertainty encodings.

papers.title: Operationalizing Trumbo's Principles of Bivariate Choropleth Map Design
papers.summary: Extends Trumbo's bivariate choropleth principles into three focal models for inverse relationships, a range of one variable within another, and direct relationships. Example obesity and inactivity maps demonstrate how palette design should follow the question a map is meant to answer.
papers.catalog_blurb: Purpose-driven focal models and palettes for bivariate choropleth maps.
key_findings: Different bivariate relationship questions call for different visual emphasis and color schemes.
The focal models connect map purpose to palette design rather than treating bivariate colors as interchangeable.
limitations: Validation is through design analysis and examples, not a new controlled user experiment.

findings.claim: The abstract defines three relationships and links each to different reader questions.
The paper summarizes the focal models and their attributes in Table 4.

sections.label: Overview
sections.description: Three focal models and design motivation.

sections.label: Model summary
sections.description: Attributes of the proposed focal models.

related.reason: Concrete bivariate color legends for climate data.
Task-based quality assessment of 2D colormaps.

papers.title: Bivariate Colour Maps for Visualizing Climate Data
papers.summary: Presents an easy-to-implement construction for sequential and diverging bivariate color legends and demonstrates it on global temperature–humidity patterns and European temperature–precipitation change. The aim is to expose spatial relationships that separate maps obscure.
papers.catalog_blurb: Constructing bivariate color legends for multivariate climate maps.
key_findings: A two-dimensional legend can combine two climate variables without discarding either variable's mapped information.
Bivariate maps condense related maps but are harder to interpret and require careful legend and palette construction.
limitations: Illustrative applications rather than perceptual validation; RGB interpolation and medium-gray center impose design constraints.

findings.claim: The abstract describes sequential and diverging legends and two climate applications.
The discussion notes both direct relationship reading and higher interpretive difficulty.

sections.label: Discussion and construction
sections.description: Benefits, difficulty, and RGB legend details.

related.reason: Purpose-driven bivariate choropleth design.
Includes and assesses Teuling palette variants.

papers.title: An Empirical Inquiry Concerning Human Understanding of Two-Variable Color Maps
papers.summary: Uses Bertin's graphical semiology to frame two experiments on how people understand two-variable color maps. It is an early argument for empirical comparison of graphical forms and for learned, semantically coherent color schemes.
papers.catalog_blurb: Early experimental study of how readers understand two-variable color maps.
key_findings: Effectiveness cannot be settled by design theory alone; competing two-variable schemes require empirical tests.
Well-learned, natural visual metaphors may support faster higher-level reading than arbitrary color assignments.
limitations: Historic experiments, printing technology, and participant expectations may not transfer directly to modern displays.

findings.claim: The opening frames two experiments as evidence for evaluating a graphical form.
The closing discussion emphasizes learning, natural metaphor, and the need for further empirical comparison.

related.reason: Modern task-based assessment of 2D colormaps.
Later operationalization of bivariate color principles.

papers.title: Fundamentals of Data Visualization
papers.summary: An example-driven handbook for matching chart form and visual encoding to the intended comparison, then refining color, uncertainty, annotation, composition, and publication output. The wiki provides a separate 29-chapter index and a catalog of source-linked design principles; use those for evidence-based review rather than treating this overview as guidance by itself.
papers.catalog_blurb: Practical handbook with detailed chapter indexes and evidence-linked figure-design principles.
key_findings: Recommendations are conditional on the data, comparison, audience, and medium; the book repeatedly presents exceptions and competing valid designs.
The design chapters cover proportional ink, overplotting, color pitfalls, redundant coding, multipanel consistency, annotation, contextual guides, final-size typography, filled marks, and 3D.
The uncertainty chapter distinguishes variability from estimate uncertainty and compares frequency framing, intervals, bands, sampled fits, and hypothetical outcome plots.
limitations: A broad instructional book, not a single empirical study; consult cited primary studies for evidence claims.

findings.claim: The book organizes chart selection around the message a figure conveys, then treats recurring design problems separately.
Wilke defines proportional ink as requiring shaded area to be directly proportional to the represented numerical value.
The uncertainty overview distinguishes compact expert displays from more intuitive frequency and animated displays for lay audiences.

Primary evaluation of HOPs discussed in the handbook.

papers.title: Regression and Other Stories
papers.authors: Andrew Gelman, Jennifer Hill, and Aki Vehtari
papers.summary: Applied handbook on regression as a tool for comparison, estimation, prediction, and causal inference. For literature-review work it is most useful for separating estimates from uncertainty, avoiding significance dichotomies, distinguishing association from causation, and checking fitted models graphically and through simulation.
papers.catalog_blurb: Applied regression handbook emphasizing uncertainty, simulation, graphical model checking, and careful interpretation.
key_findings: Model-based standard errors do not capture every source of uncertainty; bias, measurement, sampling, and modeling assumptions require separate consideration.
Regression coefficients describe conditional comparisons and should not automatically be called causal effects.
Posterior predictive checks compare observed data with replications from a fitted model to reveal discrepancies.
limitations: A broad methods textbook rather than a primary empirical study; use it for methodological framing and consult domain-specific primary evidence for substantive claims.

findings.claim: The book focuses on practical regression for comparison, estimation, prediction, and causal inference.
The authors identify bias and unmodeled uncertainty beyond model-based standard errors.
The model-checking chapter defines posterior predictive checking as comparing replicated datasets to observed data.

sections.description: Estimates, standard errors, confidence intervals, bias, and unmodeled uncertainty.

sections.description: Problems with dichotomizing results by statistical significance.

sections.label: Model checking

EEG-specific statistical modeling and uncertainty context.

papers.title: Error Bars Considered Harmful: Exploring Alternate Encodings for Mean and Error
papers.summary: Crowdsourced experiments compare conventional error bars with distributional alternatives, showing that encoding choices affect judgments and confidence and that bar-like containment can invite biased probability interpretations.
papers.catalog_blurb: Experimental evidence on error-bar biases and alternative uncertainty encodings.
key_findings: Bar-based displays produced a within-the-bar bias that symmetric distributional encodings mitigated.
Display form affected confidence and inferential strategy, so equivalent statistics are not perceptually interchangeable.
limitations: The tasks use stylized statistical displays and online participants; the two alternatives were not consistently distinguishable in performance.

findings.claim: Bar containment altered perceived likelihood.
Confidence tracked display-derived evidence imperfectly.

related.reason: Tests interpretation of error-bar-like temporal encodings.
Handbook guidance on uncertainty displays.

papers.title: Uncertainty Displays Using Quantile Dotplots or CDFs Improve Transit Decision-Making
papers.summary: A preregistered online experiment tests ten bus-arrival displays using incentivized decisions. Quantile dotplots and CDFs support decisions closer to the optimal policy and more consistent performance than common alternatives.
papers.catalog_blurb: Large incentivized study of uncertainty displays for transit decisions.
key_findings: The final analysis included 408 participants and used trial-level payoff relative to an optimal policy.
Dotplots and CDFs reached about 95% of optimal performance on the last trial.
limitations: A laboratory-style online scenario and common utility function do not reproduce every real transit context or rider preference.

findings.claim: Dotplots and CDFs achieved high and consistent final-trial decision quality.

related.reason: Evaluates sampled uncertainty displays in another decision task.

papers.title: Investigating Representation Alternatives for Communicating Uncertainty to Non-experts
papers.summary: Compares twelve weather-uncertainty representations in a 90-person survey and four selected representations in a 12-person decision game, separating subjective ratings from actual choices.
papers.catalog_blurb: Survey and small experiment on uncertainty communication to non-experts.
key_findings: More uncertainty information did not automatically improve subjective judgments or decisions.
Preference and decision performance did not align consistently.
limitations: The experiment had only 12 participants and used one simplified farming-game scenario; the PDF contains full conference proceedings.

findings.claim: The survey included 90 respondents and the game experiment 12 participants.
The authors explicitly qualify the small experiment.

related.reason: Later decision-centered evaluation with a larger sample.

papers.title: Visual Encodings of Temporal Uncertainty: A Comparative User Study
papers.summary: A within-subject user study compares six encodings for uncertain interval starts and ends across interpretation, boundary, duration, probability, and preference tasks.
papers.catalog_blurb: Task-dependent comparison of six temporal-uncertainty encodings.
key_findings: Seventy-two valid submissions showed strongly task-dependent accuracy differences.
Centered error bars produced ambiguous interpretations, while different encodings were favored for bounds versus probabilities.
limitations: Participants were visualization students, tasks used a single simplified interval, and the authors report task-design and cleaning complications.

findings.claim: Centered error bars split bounded/statistical interpretations 47%/36%, with 17% neither.

related.reason: Related evidence about error-bar interpretation.

papers.title: In Pursuit of Error: A Survey of Uncertainty Visualization Evaluation
papers.summary: A systematic survey of 86 uncertainty-visualization evaluation papers develops a six-level taxonomy connecting uncertainty inputs, displays, judgments, decisions, and outcomes.
papers.catalog_blurb: Evaluation taxonomy derived from 86 uncertainty-visualization papers.
key_findings: The review codes 372 evaluation paths across 86 publications.
The literature emphasizes constrained inputs and confirmatory accuracy more than open-ended explanation and downstream decision quality.
limitations: The taxonomy characterizes published evaluations through 2018; frequency of evaluation choices is not evidence that those choices are optimal.

findings.claim: The corpus contained 86 publications and 372 evaluation paths.

related.reason: Earlier task-centered review of uncertainty visualization assessment.

papers.title: Hypothetical Outcome Plots Help Untrained Observers Judge Trends in Ambiguous Data
papers.summary: Two crowdsourced experiments compare HOPs, error bars, and line ensembles for deciding which noisy trend generated observed data, modeling accuracy and confidence across evidence levels.
papers.catalog_blurb: Experiments on HOPs for probabilistic trend judgments by non-experts.
key_findings: HOPs supported correct trend judgments at lower evidence levels than static alternatives in the tested tasks.
Learning, presentation order, frame rate, attention, and confidence measurement qualify the result.
limitations: A single news-inspired binary trend task does not establish superiority for other uncertainty tasks or domains.

findings.claim: Experiment 1 recruited 62 MTurk Masters for two 60-trial blocks.
The authors discuss order and learning effects.

related.reason: Earlier HOP evaluation.
Related frequency-framed uncertainty display evidence.

papers.title: Practice Improves Performance of a 2D Uncertainty Integration Task Within and Across Visualizations
papers.summary: Two online experiments test whether practice improves integration of two uncertainty sources and whether learning transfers across ensemble, summary, and distributional visualizations.
papers.catalog_blurb: Evidence that practice improves and can transfer across 2D uncertainty displays.
key_findings: Experiments analyzed 118 and 56 participants.
Participants became faster and more accurate with practice, including transfer to unpracticed display types.
limitations: Online hardware and color were uncontrolled, and the integration task was abstract rather than domain-specific.

findings.claim: The abstract reports N=118 and N=56 and cross-display transfer.

related.reason: Related multi-symbol uncertainty integration task.

papers.title: Visual Semiotics & Uncertainty Visualization: An Empirical Study
papers.summary: Develops a semiotic framework for uncertainty symbols, then tests symbol intuitiveness with 72 geographically knowledgeable participants and aggregate-uncertainty judgments with 30 participants.
papers.catalog_blurb: Two experiments on intuitive and effective map uncertainty symbols.
key_findings: Fuzziness, location, and value were among the most intuitive ordinal uncertainty variables.
Intuitiveness and effectiveness were evaluated separately and did not reduce to a universal symbol ranking.
limitations: Purposeful GIS-aware samples, abstract maps, and selected symbol sets limit generalization to novices and continuous scientific fields.

findings.claim: Experiment 1 used 72 participants and 76 symbol sets.
Experiment 2 used 30 participants and 240 trials per participant.

related.reason: Tests related bivariate map uncertainty designs.

papers.title: Uncertainty in Geographic Data on Bivariate Maps: An Examination of Visualization Preference and Decision Making
papers.summary: A survey experiment compares four bivariate map encodings of geographic uncertainty, examining preferences and a decision task among college students with differing GIS knowledge.
papers.catalog_blurb: Preference and decision evidence for four bivariate uncertainty-map encodings.
key_findings: Fuzziness and lightness ranked above transparency and shape among the 37 valid preference rankings.
GIS knowledge helped performance, while preference alone did not establish decision effectiveness.
limitations: Only 37 complete rankings supported the preference comparison, and the student sample and scenario constrain generalization.

findings.claim: Mean preference ranks were fuzziness 3.35, lightness 2.97, transparency 2.38, and shape 1.30.

related.reason: Foundational empirical work on uncertainty symbol semantics.

papers.title: Human Performance and Perception of Uncertainty Visualizations in Geospatial Applications: A Scoping Review
papers.summary: A scoping review synthesizes 40 human-participant studies of geospatial uncertainty visualization, distinguishing performance, perception, preference, confidence, and decision outcomes.
papers.catalog_blurb: Recent scoping review of human evidence for geospatial uncertainty displays.
key_findings: Direct comparison evidence is sparse and heterogeneous.
Preference or reported understanding does not necessarily imply better decisions or task performance.
limitations: The review is geospatial, uses English peer-reviewed literature, and reports single-author screening as a limitation.

findings.claim: The review included 40 articles.
Preference and understanding may diverge from decision performance.

related.reason: Complementary review of evaluation pathways.
Earlier uncertainty-assessment review.

papers.title: The Current State of Uncertainty Reporting in Ecosystem Studies: A Systematic Evaluation of Peer-Reviewed Literature
papers.summary: Audits 132 ecosystem papers from 2019 for reporting of uncertainty in vegetation, soils, precipitation, and surface water. Most papers reported only a minority of relevant sources, with large differences by topic and stronger reporting when a topic was central to the paper.
papers.catalog_blurb: Systematic audit of incomplete uncertainty reporting in ecosystem science.
key_findings: Average coverage of relevant uncertainty sources ranged from 21% for precipitation to 47% for surface water.
Only 21% of papers made all data available and another 21% made some available after accounting for broken links.
limitations: Coding relevance was sometimes impossible when papers did not mention missing data, detection limits, or other practices.

findings.claim: The abstract reports topic-specific uncertainty coverage and data-availability rates.
Sampling error was the most commonly reported source across the assessed disciplines.
